title: What is a caravan in law
paras: So — what is a caravan in law? The 1960 legislation defines it as a structure designed or adapted for human habitation, capable of being moved from one place to another, whether towed or carried on a vehicle or trailer. So it must be for living in — appearance is irrelevant, which is why containers and converted horseboxes are tested on the definition, not on looks. It must be movable. And it's expressly not a building — a chattel, unless installation tips into building operations. The precise references sit in the written guide; I'll keep us on the ideas.

"Capable of being moved" is physical capability, not convenience — the case is Bunn: movable without structural damage by normal methods, towing, craning, a low-loader. No wheels or regular movement needed, and highway-legality is beside the point. What defeats mobility is physical: brick skirts tied in, bolts through the chassis, deep concrete bases, porches or steps built in so removal means demolition.

Inspectors run three tests — size, construction and assembly, and mobility — all must be met. Fail one and it isn't a caravan: presumptively a building, its siting operational development needing permission unless a permitted development right applies, with a floor-area fee and far easier enforcement. Pass all three and it's a caravan, usually a chattel, whose siting isn't development unless the use of the land materially changes. And keep the regimes apart: the caravan legislation defines the caravan and runs site licensing but grants no planning permission; the planning Act regulates development and ignores the licence, so a notice citing licensing breaches has already misstepped.

title: Twin units and the size limits
paras: Now, twin units and the size limits. The 1968 Act extends the definition to twin-units — homes too big to move in one piece — adding three tests. No more than two sections, built separately and designed to assemble on site. Joined only by bolts, clamps or similar — the final assembly a simple mechanical joining, not construction like building a house. And movable once assembled, even if the move needs a special escort.

The dimensions, last set in 2006: twenty metres long excluding the drawbar, six point eight wide, three point oh five internal height to the living accommodation. Over any one and it's a building unless you show otherwise — a tiny breach is fatal, three point oh seven fails. The roof void doesn't count towards that height, which has decided appeals. And on construction, the test won't tolerate on-site welding, cutting and reframing walls or floors, traditional building methods, brickwork skirting as permanent support, or deep concrete foundations — the classic failures being halves that then need internal walls or pads poured specially.

Singles and twins differ. A single arrives complete, so it turns on mobility after installation, failing when the install's too permanent. Twins drive most appeals, hanging on that assembly test. On supports, non-permanent systems — jack legs, proprietary pads — aren't foundations, and aren't a structural third section; the line between those and poured bases is often the whole case.

title: When a caravan is development
paras: So when is a caravan development? The planning Act's two limbs — operational development and material change of use — give the two questions: is the caravan a building, or installed by building operations, and does its use materially change the use of the land? It can meet every limb of the caravan definition and still be development by either route. Measor settled that one meeting the definition normally isn't a building — it lacks permanence, moving without demolition — but it didn't say a caravan can never be one.

The Carter and Byrne line asks whether the installation itself is building operations: deep or continuous foundations, anchors into the ground, structural brick skirting, permanent buried services you can't remove, integrated porches, decking or extensions, or a structure removable only by dismantling beyond the separation the twin-unit rules permit — permanence leaning on Barvis and Elitestone: size, permanence, attachment. A caravan can also be development through use: a new planning unit forms once it has its own curtilage, parking or access and runs as an independent household; residential use on agricultural land is almost always a material change; and intensification — more units, or year-round occupation of a seasonal site — shifts the character even where each unit alone is lawful.

Two points from the appeal record. Intention to move is irrelevant — a twin-unit on jacks nobody meant to move was still a caravan, while an identical annexe on poured pads, with a sub-frame and fixed steps, was a building. And evidence decides it: the neighbours' construction photographs beat generic factory images.

title: Ancillary caravan or independent dwelling
paras: Ancillary caravan, or independent dwelling? Start with curtilage — factual, not a legal fiction: the land immediately around a dwelling, used for purposes intimately tied to its enjoyment, judged on layout, functional association, patterns of use and enclosure. Land Registry boundaries don't come into it. A caravan within the curtilage may share the planning unit; one in the paddock beyond almost always creates a new use of land once it's lived in. And keep the terms precise: incidental use — a home office, the odd guest — and ancillary use — accommodation supporting the main dwelling — differ, and both differ from independence.

The planning unit test comes from Burdle: the unit of occupation, and the purpose the land's used for. A separate unit — and development — forms where occupation goes autonomous: its own access, garden, parking, postal identity, separate metering, a domestic life of its own; there's no new unit where it stays part of the same household, with nothing fenced off and no independent servicing. The sharpest question: would the caravan still work as a home if the main dwelling were removed? Facilities don't decide independence; patterns of occupation do.

Temporary siting during a self-build recurs. The touring caravan is almost certainly lawful as a structure — the question is whether occupation is genuinely temporary and tied to the works, or has drifted into a new residential use of the land. Minimal supports, moving it as construction requires, and removal at completion point one way; multi-year settled family occupation the other. Staff accommodation on commercial, equestrian or agricultural land is the same — the stationing is a change of use needing its own justification, however lawful the business.

title: The 28-day rule and PD routes
paras: Now the twenty-eight-day rule and the permitted development routes. Two first principles. These rights apply only to actual development — so if the siting isn't development, because it's a caravan, ancillary, the same planning unit, permitted development is irrelevant: it's already lawful. And P-D doesn't override site licensing or the caravan analysis; it bites only where the siting is development and you're leaning on it to avoid express permission.

The one everyone reaches for is the twenty-eight-day right — use of land for any purpose for up to twenty-eight days a calendar year, aggregate not consecutive, a right over the land, not the caravan. It covers temporary events, seasonal activities, the odd touring visitor, but doesn't permit operational development, gives no right to live in a caravan for twenty-eight days, and can't be stretched into quasi-permanent occupation by rolling declarations or rotating units through one pitch. A separate temporary right covers moveable structures required for the duration of operations on that or adjoining land, but the caravan must be genuinely required by the works and falls away when they finish — a family home through a two-year self-build won't qualify, being residential.

For caravans specifically, the sharper route is the caravan-site right for licence-exempt circumstances — in particular building and engineering sites. A caravan accommodating someone employed in connection with the operations on that or adjoining land needs neither a site licence nor express permission for the caravan-site use, as long as the works run. "Employed" is undefined and read fairly liberally, but the accommodation must be genuinely tied to the operations, and the right falls away, caravans removed, once works cease.

And a warning. Agricultural permitted development doesn't authorise residential use of caravans, nor statics as workers' dwellings — at most, narrowly, a caravan as a temporary agricultural structure, not habitation. No temporary route authorises the operational development that comes with caravans — bases, foundations, drainage, hardstanding, decking — each needs its own justification. Nor does P-D ever permit a material change to a new dwellinghouse, or a separate planning unit.

title: LDCs, enforcement and the myths
paras: Finally — certificates, enforcement, and the myths. Certificates matter more here than almost anywhere, because appearance misleads and the questions are ones of fact. An existing-use certificate is proved on the balance of probabilities: the physical characteristics, how it was installed at siting, the pattern and nature of use — ancillary or independent — the duration where immunity is claimed, the planning unit, and the absence of building operations. A proposed-development certificate is forward-looking, letting method statements, drawings and mobility evidence be weighed before siting. The predictable refusals: rejecting it because the unit might be lived in independently, treating bedrooms and bathrooms as inherently a dwelling, misunderstanding the final act of assembly, and conflating licensing with planning.

Enforcement must target the correct breach — the commonest cause of failure at appeal. Where occupation is independent, residential use has begun on agricultural land, or numbers have intensified the use, allege a material change of use to stationing a caravan for residential purposes. Where foundations, sub-frames, structural skirting or attached works have turned siting into construction, allege erection of a building. And where the caravan is lawful but the works beneath aren't, a split notice — removing the works, allowing the caravan — avoids overreach.

Route and fee follow the same analysis. Caravan plus ancillary use, and the certificate is cleanest and cheapest. Any development element — oversize, building-level assembly, foundations, an independent unit — needs a full application at the full fee. Misclassify it and you store up validation and Community Infrastructure Levy problems: a genuine caravan attracts no levy, but a structure that's in law a building, or a use creating a dwellinghouse, engages it. Fee strategy is part of the legal assessment, not a late procedural step.
